alcohol-in-pregnancy.title: Alcohol in pregnancy
alcohol-in-pregnancy.glance: The safest approach is not to drink any alcohol in pregnancy or when trying to conceive.
alcohol-in-pregnancy.overview:
The NHS advice is clear and simple: the safest approach is **not to drink alcohol at all** if you're
pregnant or trying to conceive. Not drinking keeps any risk to your baby to a minimum.

The reason is that alcohol passes from your blood, through the placenta, to your baby — whose liver
isn't developed enough to process it. Drinking in pregnancy can lead to fetal alcohol spectrum
disorder (FASD), a range of lifelong difficulties with learning, behaviour, and development.

If you drank before you knew you were pregnant, try not to worry: the risk to the baby from small
amounts early on is likely to be low. The helpful thing is simply to avoid alcohol for the rest of
the pregnancy from now on.
alcohol-in-pregnancy.when_to_see_doctor:
- If you're finding it hard to stop drinking, that's nothing to be ashamed of — tell your midwife or
  GP. They can offer support without judgement, and getting help is good for you and your baby.

antenatal-care.title: Antenatal care
antenatal-care.glance: Antenatal care is the regular check-ups through pregnancy that help keep you and your baby well.
antenatal-care.overview:
Antenatal care is the care you get during pregnancy to keep you and your baby as healthy as
possible. You'll usually see a midwife, and a doctor too if you need one. It's worth starting early:
contact your midwife or GP as soon as you know you're pregnant.

Your first proper appointment — the "booking appointment" — is usually between 8 and 12 weeks. After
that you're offered regular check-ups: at least 10 appointments and 2 ultrasound scans if it's your
first baby, or around 7 if you've given birth before, with more towards the end.

At these visits your midwife checks your blood pressure and urine, measures your bump to follow your
baby's growth, offers screening tests, and talks with you about your baby's movements and how you're
feeling. Many important things — like pre-eclampsia or gestational diabetes — are picked up here
before you'd notice anything, which is exactly why the appointments matter.
antenatal-care.when_to_see_doctor:
- Contact a **midwife or GP as soon as you find out you're pregnant** so your care can start early —
  ideally in time for that first appointment before around 10 to 12 weeks.
- Try to keep **all** your antenatal appointments, even if you feel completely well — several checks
  are designed to catch silent problems early.

babys-movements.title: Your baby's movements
babys-movements.glance: Feeling your baby move is a sign they're well — if the movements slow or change, call your midwife straight away.
babys-movements.overview:
Feeling your baby move is one of the reassuring signs that they're doing well. Most people start to
feel movements somewhere between 16 and 24 weeks of pregnancy — often later in a first pregnancy, so
after 20 weeks is common the first time around.

There's no set number of movements you "should" feel, and no need to count kicks against a target.
Every baby is different, and what matters is getting to know **your** baby's own usual pattern
through the day — the times they're active and the times they're quiet.

Once you know that pattern, a change from it is the thing to pay attention to. Trust what you know
about your own baby.
babys-movements.when_to_see_doctor:
Getting to know your baby's normal pattern is what lets you notice a change. If you're ever unsure
whether movements have slowed or changed, it is always right to call and check — you will never be
wasting anyone's time.
babys-movements.red_flags:
- If your baby is **moving less than usual, their movements change, or you can't feel them moving**,
  **call your midwife or maternity unit immediately** — at any time of day or night. **Do not wait
  until the next day**, even if it's the middle of the night.
- Do not rely on a home heartbeat monitor (doppler) or an app to reassure yourself — get checked in
  person.

back-pain-in-pregnancy.title: Back pain in pregnancy
back-pain-in-pregnancy.glance: Back pain is very common in pregnancy as ligaments soften and your bump grows — usually harmless.
back-pain-in-pregnancy.overview:
Back pain is one of the most common parts of pregnancy. As your body gets ready for birth, the
ligaments naturally soften and stretch, and your growing bump changes how you carry your weight —
both of which put extra strain on your lower back and pelvis.

Everyday things can ease it: being mindful of your posture when standing, sitting and lifting;
wearing flat, supportive shoes; a firm mattress or a supportive pillow; and gentle, regular movement
like walking, pregnancy yoga, or exercises from a class. If it's really getting in the way, an
obstetric physiotherapist can give tailored advice.

Most pregnancy back pain is nothing to worry about — but a few patterns are worth getting checked
promptly, which is what the guidance below is for.
back-pain-in-pregnancy.when_to_see_doctor:
Contact your **GP or midwife** promptly if your back pain:

- is **severe**, or comes on in the **second or third trimester** (it can sometimes be a sign of
  early labour)
- comes with a **fever, vaginal bleeding, or pain when you pee**
- is **in your side(s), under your ribs**
back-pain-in-pregnancy.red_flags:
- Call **999 or go to A&E** if you **lose feeling in your legs, buttocks, or genitals**, or lose
  control of your bladder or bowels. This is rare, but needs emergency care.

basal-body-temperature.title: Basal body temperature
basal-body-temperature.glance: Basal body temperature is your at-rest morning temperature, which rises slightly after ovulation.
basal-body-temperature.overview:
Basal body temperature (BBT) is your body's temperature fully at rest. Measured the same way each
day, it shows a small but telling change across the cycle: after ovulation, it rises a little and
stays up until your next period.

The rise is small — around 0.4 to 0.8°F (roughly 0.2 to 0.4°C) — so it's read from a pattern over
several days, not a single reading. To catch it, you take your temperature each morning before
getting up, eating or drinking, ideally at the same time. Almost everyone has ovulated within about
three days of the temperature climbing.

Because the rise comes *after* the egg is released, BBT confirms that ovulation has happened rather
than predicting it in advance. Over a few cycles it can help you see the shape of your own cycle,
though on its own it isn't a precise way to catch the fertile days.
basal-body-temperature.deep:
BBT is one of the fertility-awareness signs recorded daily, together with cervical mucus and cycle
length. It pairs naturally with mucus tracking: the change to clear, slippery mucus suggests the
fertile window is opening, while the temperature rise a few days later confirms ovulation has
passed. Many things can nudge a resting temperature — poor sleep, illness, alcohol, or a lie-in —
so single odd readings matter less than the overall trend.

bleeding-in-pregnancy.title: Bleeding in pregnancy
bleeding-in-pregnancy.glance: Bleeding in pregnancy isn't always serious — light spotting is common early on — but always get it checked.
bleeding-in-pregnancy.overview:
Bleeding from the vagina during pregnancy is not always a sign that something is wrong. Light
bleeding or spotting is fairly common in early pregnancy in particular, and many pregnancies continue
perfectly well after it.

That said, bleeding can sometimes be a sign of a problem — such as a miscarriage or an ectopic
pregnancy — so it's the kind of thing that should **always be checked**, whatever the amount. Getting
it looked at is how the cause is found and how you get the right care quickly if you need it.

Because the same symptom can mean very different things, the useful step isn't to guess — it's to
make contact and be seen.
bleeding-in-pregnancy.when_to_see_doctor:
- **Always contact your maternity unit** (or, if you're less than 20 weeks or don't have their
  number, an early pregnancy unit or **NHS 111**) if you have **any** vaginal bleeding in pregnancy,
  even light spotting — so the cause can be checked.
bleeding-in-pregnancy.red_flags:
- Call **999 or go to A&E** if you have **heavy bleeding** — for example soaking a pad soon after
  putting it on — especially with **severe tummy pain, shoulder-tip pain, or feeling sick, faint,
  dizzy, or losing consciousness.** This needs emergency care.

breast-awareness.title: Breast awareness
breast-awareness.glance: Breast awareness is simply knowing how your breasts normally look and feel, so you notice changes.
breast-awareness.overview:
Breast awareness isn't a special technique — it's just getting to know what's normal for you, so
that anything new stands out. Checking your breasts or chest regularly helps you learn their usual
look and feel; once a month is a good rhythm.

There's no single "right" way. Many people look in the mirror with arms down and then raised, and
feel each breast, up into the armpit. What you're building is familiarity, not a diagnosis — the
goal is just to notice a change early if one happens.

Breasts also change naturally across the cycle and through life, so some changes are completely
normal. The point of awareness is knowing your own normal well enough to spot something that isn't.
breast-awareness.when_to_see_doctor:
See a GP if you notice any change that isn't normal for you, such as:

- a lump or swelling in your breast, chest, or armpit
- a change in the skin, like dimpling (it can look like orange peel) or redness
- a change in the size or shape of one or both breasts
- nipple discharge (if you're not pregnant or breastfeeding), which may have blood in it
- a change in the look of your nipple, such as it turning inwards
- pain in your breast or armpit that doesn't go away

Most breast changes are not cancer and turn out to be harmless — but it's always worth getting a
change checked promptly, because if something does need attention, finding it early helps.

breastfeeding.title: Breastfeeding
breastfeeding.glance: Breast milk protects a baby from infections and adapts as they grow — and any amount has benefits.
breastfeeding.overview:
Breast milk is a natural, complete food for a baby: it provides the nutrition, vitamins and minerals
they need, and it changes over time to match their stage. It also helps protect against infections
and illnesses, and offers some longer-term health benefits.

There are benefits for the person feeding, too — breastfeeding is linked with a lower risk of breast
and ovarian cancer, among other things — and the general pattern is that the more and longer you
breastfeed, the greater the benefits. Importantly, **any** amount of breast milk is worthwhile; it's
not all-or-nothing.

Feeding a baby can also be harder than expected at first, and that's common. Help is available — from
your midwife, health visitor, and NHS feeding support — so reaching out early if it's not going
smoothly is a good move.
breastfeeding.when_to_see_doctor:
- Ask your **midwife or health visitor** for help early if feeding is painful or difficult, or
  you're worried your baby isn't getting enough — support can make a real difference.
- How you feed your baby is a personal decision, and support is there whatever you choose; what
  matters is that you and your baby are well.

cervical-mucus.title: Cervical mucus
cervical-mucus.glance: Cervical mucus is the natural discharge that changes through the cycle and marks your fertile days.
cervical-mucus.overview:
Cervical mucus is the fluid the cervix makes, which you may notice as discharge. It's normal, and
its look and feel change in a fairly predictable pattern across the cycle — which is why it's one
of the signs used to spot the fertile days.

Just after a period there are often a few "dry" days with little mucus. As an egg begins to
mature, mucus increases and tends to be white or yellow, cloudy and sticky. In the days right
before ovulation it usually turns clear, wet and slippery, stretching between the fingers like raw
egg white — this is the most fertile time. After ovulation it typically becomes sticky and cloudy
again, or dries up.

Everyone's pattern is a little different, and it can take a few cycles of paying attention to learn
your own. Some things — such as hormonal contraception, breastfeeding, or an infection — can change
the mucus, so it isn't a reliable fertility sign for everyone.
cervical-mucus.deep:
Reading cervical mucus is one of the fertility-awareness signs people track, alongside resting body
temperature and cycle length; learning them usually takes two to three cycles. Unlike a temperature
rise, which confirms ovulation only after it has happened, the shift to clear, slippery, egg-white
mucus tends to appear *before* ovulation, which is why it's used to flag the fertile window as it
opens rather than after it closes.

cervical-screening.title: Cervical screening (smear test)
cervical-screening.glance: Cervical screening is a routine check of the health of your cervix that helps prevent cervical cancer.
cervical-screening.overview:
Cervical screening is a test that checks the health of the cervix — the opening to the womb at the
top of the vagina. It isn't a test for cancer. Instead, it's a way to spot changes early and help
prevent cervical cancer from developing in the first place.

Everyone with a cervix is invited from the age of 25 up to 64. You're sent an invitation when
you're due, at regular intervals, so you don't need to remember to book it out of the blue —
though it's always your choice whether to go.

The test itself is quick and done by a nurse. Many people feel a bit nervous about it, which is
completely understandable; knowing what it's for — a routine, preventive check — can make it feel
more manageable.
cervical-screening.when_to_see_doctor:
- Screening is for when you **don't** have symptoms. If you notice something that worries you
  between screenings — such as unusual bleeding (between periods, after sex, or after menopause) —
  see a GP rather than waiting for your next invitation.
- If you've been invited and you're unsure or anxious about going, it's worth talking to your GP or
  practice nurse, who can explain what happens and answer your questions.

combined-pill.title: The combined pill
combined-pill.glance: The combined pill is a daily pill with two hormones that mainly works by stopping ovulation.
combined-pill.overview:
The combined pill is a daily tablet containing two hormones — versions of estrogen and progestogen,
similar to the ones the ovaries make. It's one of the most familiar forms of contraception.

It prevents pregnancy in a few ways at once. Mainly, it stops the ovaries from releasing an egg
(ovulation). It also thickens the mucus at the neck of the womb, making it harder for sperm to get
through, and thins the lining of the womb.

How well it works depends on taking it as directed: it's over 99% effective with perfect use, but
with typical, everyday use — where pills are sometimes missed or delayed — it's around 91%
effective. Like most methods, it doesn't protect against STIs, so some people use condoms as well.
combined-pill.deep:
The combined pill is usually taken in a pattern across the month, and how to take it, who it suits,
and its side effects and risks are things a clinician goes through when it's prescribed — it's not
suitable for everyone. Because it's a daily method, its real-world effectiveness leans a lot on
routine. This atom explains what it is and how it works; the specifics of starting, taking, or
stopping it are a conversation with a GP, nurse, or pharmacist.

common-pregnancy-symptoms.title: Common pregnancy symptoms
common-pregnancy-symptoms.glance: Pregnancy brings lots of small aches and changes — mostly normal, though a few are worth checking.
common-pregnancy-symptoms.overview:
Pregnancy is a lot of change for your body, and it comes with a long list of everyday niggles. Most
are common and not a sign that anything is wrong — they're just part of growing a baby.

Familiar ones include backache, heartburn and indigestion, constipation, piles, swollen ankles, feet
and fingers, tiredness and broken sleep, leg cramp, headaches, feeling faint, and more discharge than
usual. Many ease with small comfort measures, and your midwife can suggest what's safe if something's
bothering you.

The useful thing is knowing which changes are the ordinary kind and which ones are worth flagging —
because a few symptoms, though less common, do need checking rather than waiting out.
common-pregnancy-symptoms.when_to_see_doctor:
Most of these are normal, but contact your **midwife or maternity unit** promptly if you have:

- **vaginal bleeding**, or a sudden gush or trickle of fluid
- your **baby moving less** than usual
- a **severe headache, vision problems, or sudden swelling** of the face, hands or feet (possible
  signs of pre-eclampsia)
- **severe or one-sided tummy pain**, or a **high temperature**
- **itching**, especially on your hands and feet or that's worse at night (it can be a sign of a
  liver condition in pregnancy that needs checking)

condoms.title: Condoms
condoms.glance: Condoms are a barrier method — and the only kind of contraception that also protects against STIs.
condoms.overview:
A condom is a thin barrier — usually latex, or a plastic alternative for those with a latex allergy
— worn on the penis during sex. It works simply: it stops sperm from entering the vagina.

What makes condoms special among contraceptives is that they're **the only method that also protects
against sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including HIV.** That's why they're often used
alongside another method — one for pregnancy, both together for infection protection.

Used correctly every time, condoms are about 98% effective at preventing pregnancy. With typical
use — where they're sometimes used incorrectly or not every time — that drops to around 82%. Using
one properly and consistently is what makes the difference.
condoms.deep:
Because condoms are used in the moment rather than in advance, their real-world effectiveness
depends heavily on consistent, correct use. Internal condoms (worn inside the vagina) are another
barrier option. Unlike most methods, condoms need no prescription and are widely available, and
their dual role — pregnancy and STI protection — is why they come up so often in conversations about
safer sex.

contraception.title: Contraception
contraception.glance: Contraception is the different ways to prevent pregnancy — and there are many to choose from.
contraception.overview:
Contraception — sometimes called birth control — is the range of methods used to prevent pregnancy.
There are many of them, and they work in different ways: some use hormones, some are barriers, some
sit inside the womb, and some are based on tracking the cycle.

How well a method works depends a lot on how it's used. Some methods — like the implant and the
coils — are "fit and forget," and are over 99% effective. Others, like the pill or condoms, are
very effective when used perfectly, but a bit less so with everyday, typical use, because it's
easier to forget a pill or use a condom incorrectly.

One thing worth knowing: **only condoms also protect against sexually transmitted infections
(STIs)**. The other methods prevent pregnancy but not infection, which is why condoms are sometimes
used alongside another method.

There's no single "best" method — the right one depends on your health, your body, and what fits
your life. A GP or a sexual health clinic can talk you through the options and help you choose.
contraception.deep:
Because methods differ so much, it helps to think about what matters to you: how effective it is,
whether it involves remembering something daily, how long it lasts, whether you want hormones or
not, and whether STI protection matters for your situation. Many people change methods over their
life as their needs change. This knowledge base describes how the common methods work so the
choices feel clearer — but the decision, and any prescription or fitting, is one to make with a
clinician.

contraceptive-implant.title: The contraceptive implant
contraceptive-implant.glance: The implant is a tiny rod placed in the upper arm that releases a hormone for a few years.
contraceptive-implant.overview:
The contraceptive implant is a small, flexible rod — about the size of a matchstick — placed just
under the skin of the upper arm by a trained clinician. Once in, it steadily releases a progestogen
hormone and works for up to about three years.

It prevents pregnancy mainly by stopping the ovaries from releasing an egg (ovulation), and by
thickening the mucus at the neck of the womb so sperm can't get through. Because there's nothing to
remember day to day, it's one of the "fit and forget" methods.

That's also why it's one of the most reliable options: the implant is over 99% effective, and its
effectiveness barely changes between perfect and typical use. Like other hormonal methods, it
doesn't protect against STIs.
contraceptive-implant.deep:
The implant is a long-acting reversible method — it keeps working until it's removed, and fertility
returns after removal. Having it fitted and taken out are quick procedures done by a clinician, who
also talks through who it suits and its side effects. This atom explains what it is and how it
works; the decision to have one is a conversation with a GP, nurse, or sexual health clinic.

cycle-and-your-wellbeing.title: Your cycle & your wellbeing
cycle-and-your-wellbeing.glance: Your cycle is a bit like a monthly check-in on your health — changes in it can be worth noticing.
cycle-and-your-wellbeing.overview:
Your menstrual cycle isn't separate from the rest of your health — it's connected to it. A cycle
that's regular for you is generally a sign that your body is ticking along as it should. That's why
some people think of the period as a kind of monthly signal about overall wellbeing.

Everyday life plays into it. Body weight is one example: being significantly under- or over-weight
can affect the hormones that drive ovulation, which can make periods irregular. This works both
ways — looking after the basics, like a balanced approach to eating and staying active, supports the
cycle, and a steady cycle is a sign those things are in reasonable balance.

This isn't about chasing a "perfect" cycle or blaming yourself for changes. It's simply that
paying gentle attention to your cycle can be a useful window into how you're doing — and a prompt to
check in with a clinician if something shifts.
cycle-and-your-wellbeing.when_to_see_doctor:
- See a GP if your periods become irregular, stop, or change in a way that's not usual for you —
  ongoing changes can sometimes point to something worth looking into.
- It's also worth a conversation if period problems are affecting your daily life, so you can get
  support rather than just putting up with them.

ectopic-pregnancy.title: Ectopic pregnancy
ectopic-pregnancy.glance: An ectopic pregnancy grows outside the womb — it can't continue and needs prompt medical care.
ectopic-pregnancy.overview:
An ectopic pregnancy is when a fertilised egg implants outside the womb, most often in one of the
fallopian tubes. Sadly, a pregnancy in this position can't develop into a baby, and it can't be
moved into the womb — so it always needs treating.

Signs usually show up between about weeks 4 and 12, and can include tummy pain low down on one side,
vaginal bleeding or a brown watery discharge, pain in the tip of your shoulder, or discomfort when
you pee or poo. The mix of symptoms varies, and some can be easy to mistake for something minor,
which is why getting them checked matters.

It's an uncommon situation, but a potentially serious one, so it's not something to wait out. Getting
advice early means it can be looked after safely.
ectopic-pregnancy.when_to_see_doctor:
- Contact your GP or call **NHS 111** if you have a combination of these symptoms **and you might be
  pregnant** — even if you haven't had a positive pregnancy test. It's important to get advice right
  away.
ectopic-pregnancy.red_flags:
- Call **999 or go to A&E** if you have a **sudden, sharp, intense pain in your tummy**, feel **very
  dizzy or faint**, look **very pale**, or feel sick with these. This can mean the fallopian tube
  has ruptured — a medical emergency that needs urgent treatment.

emergency-contraception.title: Emergency contraception
emergency-contraception.glance: Emergency contraception can prevent pregnancy after unprotected sex — and the sooner, the better.
emergency-contraception.overview:
Emergency contraception is a way to prevent pregnancy after sex without contraception, or when your
usual method may have failed (a missed pill, a split condom). There are two kinds, and timing
matters for both.

The first is the **emergency pill**. There are two types: one (levonorgestrel) can be taken up to
3 days — 72 hours — after sex, and another (ulipristal acetate, brand name ellaOne) up to 5 days —
120 hours. The second option is the **copper coil (IUD)**, which a clinician can fit up to 5 days
after sex; it's the most effective form of emergency contraception, and it can then stay in as
ongoing contraception if you'd like.

For all of these, **the sooner you use them, the better they tend to work** — so it's worth acting
quickly rather than waiting. You can get emergency contraception from a pharmacy, a GP, a sexual
health clinic, or a walk-in centre, often free.
emergency-contraception.when_to_see_doctor:
- Because it's time-sensitive, don't wait — a pharmacist can provide the emergency pill quickly, and
  a sexual health clinic or GP can fit the IUD.
- Emergency contraception is about preventing pregnancy, not infection. If there's any chance of a
  sexually transmitted infection, a sexual health clinic can advise on testing.
- If your period is then more than a few days late, or very different from usual, it's worth taking
  a pregnancy test and speaking to a clinician.

endometriosis.title: Endometriosis
endometriosis.glance: Endometriosis is a condition where tissue like the womb lining grows outside the womb, often causing pain.
endometriosis.overview:
Endometriosis is a long-term condition where cells similar to the lining of the womb (uterus) grow
in other parts of the body, such as around the ovaries, the pelvis, or the bowel. It's common —
estimated to affect around 1 in 10 women of reproductive age worldwide.

Because this tissue behaves a little like the womb lining, it can cause inflammation and, over time,
scar tissue. The most common sign is pain: often severe period pain, but also pelvic or lower-back
pain at other times, pain during or after sex, and pain when peeing or pooing. Very heavy periods,
deep tiredness, low mood, and difficulty getting pregnant are also common. Symptoms vary a lot —
some people have severe pain, others little.

Endometriosis is often misunderstood and can take years to recognise, partly because period pain is
so often dismissed as "normal." Severe pain that disrupts your life is not something you simply have
to put up with — it's worth taking seriously.
endometriosis.deep:
The exact cause of endometriosis isn't known, and there's currently no cure — but treatments can
help manage the symptoms, and support ranges from medicines to, for some people, surgery, alongside
help for the physical and emotional toll. One of the biggest challenges is delay: on average it can
take several years, sometimes many, to reach a diagnosis. That's part of why keeping a clear record
of your symptoms, and returning to a clinician if you're not being heard, can matter so much.
endometriosis.when_to_see_doctor:
It's worth seeing a GP if:

- you have severe period pain that stops you doing normal activities
- your periods are very heavy — for example, needing to change a pad or tampon every 1–2 hours
- you have ongoing pelvic or lower-back pain, pain during or after sex, or pain when peeing or pooing
- you're finding it hard to get pregnant
- treatment you've already had hasn't helped, or your symptoms have got worse

Because endometriosis can take time to diagnose, it's okay to go back if your symptoms aren't taken
seriously — a clear picture of your pain over time helps. If the pain or heavy bleeding is also
affecting your mood, tell your GP; that's part of the picture, and support is available.

estrogen.title: Estrogen
estrogen.glance: Estrogen is a key hormone that helps prepare your body for a possible pregnancy each cycle.
estrogen.overview:
Estrogen is one of the main hormones behind the menstrual cycle. In the first half of the cycle
(the follicular phase) its level rises as a follicle in the ovary matures. This rise thickens the
lining of the uterus and leads up to ovulation.

Estrogen also influences things you might notice day to day — energy, mood, and changes in
cervical mucus around your fertile days. After ovulation its level dips and then shifts again,
working alongside another hormone, progesterone, through the second half of the cycle.

Levels naturally rise and fall across each cycle, and they change across life stages too. This is
normal — it's the rhythm your body runs on, not something to "fix."
estrogen.deep:
Estrogen isn't a single substance but a group of related hormones (the most active in the cycle
is estradiol). Most of it is made by the ovaries, in the growing follicle. Its cyclical rise and
fall — together with progesterone, and the brain's signalling hormones LH and FSH — is what
drives the phases of the cycle. Because estrogen touches many systems, its natural shifts can
show up in small ways throughout the month; tracking helps you learn your own pattern rather than
compare it to an "average."

exercise-and-your-cycle.title: Movement & your cycle
exercise-and-your-cycle.glance: You can stay active all through your cycle — and regular movement may ease cramps and PMS.
exercise-and-your-cycle.overview:
You can be physically active at any point in your cycle. Some people find they have more energy and
can push a little harder at certain times of the month, and less at others — both are normal, and
neither is a reason to stop moving.

Regular activity can actually help with some period-related symptoms. People who exercise regularly
often have fewer painful cramps, and staying active may ease premenstrual symptoms (PMS) too. On
lower-energy days, gentler movement still counts — it doesn't have to be intense to be worthwhile.

There's no need to schedule your life around your cycle, and no single "right" way to move. Noticing
your own energy pattern across the month can simply help you plan in a way that feels good.
exercise-and-your-cycle.when_to_see_doctor:
- Very heavy training, or exercising so much that your body runs low on energy, can make periods
  become irregular or stop altogether. A regular cycle is generally a sign that things are ticking
  along well, so it's worth talking to a GP if your periods become irregular or stop — this can be
  connected to bone and hormone health over time.

exercise-in-pregnancy.title: Exercise in pregnancy
exercise-in-pregnancy.glance: Staying active is safe and good in most pregnancies — gently, without exhausting yourself.
exercise-in-pregnancy.overview:
Keeping active in pregnancy is good for you and isn't dangerous for your baby — in fact, staying fit
can help you cope with the changes ahead and with labour. You don't need to take up anything intense;
carrying on with your normal daily activity, as long as it feels comfortable, is a fine starting
point.

A simple rule of thumb: you should be able to **hold a conversation** as you move. If you're too
breathless to talk, ease off. Gentle options like walking, swimming, aqua-natal classes, and
pregnancy yoga suit most people. If you weren't active before, this isn't the time to begin a
strenuous new routine — build up gently instead.

A few activities are best avoided or approached with care — such as lying flat on your back after
around 16 weeks, contact sports, scuba diving, and anything with a real risk of falling.
exercise-in-pregnancy.when_to_see_doctor:
- Check with your **midwife** before starting a new aerobic exercise programme, or if you have a
  health condition or pregnancy concern.
- **Stop and get advice** if you feel unwell, dizzy or very breathless, or if you have any pain,
  bleeding, or contractions while exercising.

fertile-window.title: The fertile window
fertile-window.glance: The fertile window is the handful of days each cycle when sex can lead to pregnancy.
fertile-window.overview:
The fertile window is the short stretch of the cycle when pregnancy is possible. It exists because
of two timings that don't quite line up: an egg can only be fertilised for about 12 to 24 hours
after it's released, but sperm can survive inside the body for several days — up to about a week —
waiting for an egg.

Put together, that means the window opens a few days before ovulation and closes about a day
after it. In practice you're most fertile in the 2 to 3 days leading up to ovulation and on the
day itself, because sperm can already be there when the egg arrives.

Since ovulation can shift from cycle to cycle, the fertile window moves too. That's why it's
usually thought of as a range of days rather than a single date, and why tracking signs across
several cycles is more dependable than counting on one calendar calculation.
fertile-window.deep:
The exact days differ from person to person and month to month, so the window is best estimated
from the body's own signals rather than a fixed formula. Changes in cervical mucus point to the
window opening as ovulation approaches, and a rise in resting body temperature confirms — after
the fact — that ovulation has passed and the window has closed. Ovulation predictor kits work a
step earlier, detecting the surge in luteinizing hormone (LH) that comes shortly before the egg is
released.

first-period.title: Starting periods (first period)
first-period.glance: Your first period usually arrives around age 12 — anywhere from about 8 to 17 is normal.
first-period.overview:
Your first period — sometimes called menarche — is when the menstrual cycle begins for the first
time. Most people start around age 12, but anywhere from about 8 to 17 is normal. It often comes
roughly two years after your breasts start to develop.

There are usually signs in the lead-up: growing underarm and pubic hair, and a little clear or
white discharge in the months before. Knowing these are coming can make the first period feel less
sudden.

At the start, periods are often irregular — the gaps can be long or short, and it can take your
body several months, even a couple of years, to settle into a steadier rhythm. Once it does,
periods tend to come somewhere around every 23 to 35 days and last about 2 to 7 days. Early
irregularity is normal and not something to worry about.
first-period.when_to_see_doctor:
- See a GP if periods **have not started by age 15**, or by **13 if there are no other signs of
  puberty** (like breast development or body hair). This is just to check things are developing as
  expected — usually everything is fine.

folic-acid.title: Folic acid & vitamins in pregnancy
folic-acid.glance: Folic acid before and in early pregnancy helps protect the baby — plus a daily vitamin D.
folic-acid.overview:
Two supplements really matter in pregnancy, and the NHS recommends both.

**Folic acid** is the big one. Taking a 400 microgram supplement every day — ideally from before you
conceive (about three months ahead) and until the end of the first trimester, at 12 weeks — helps
protect the baby against neural tube defects such as spina bifida. Because it works so early, it's
one of the few things worth starting *before* a pregnancy if you're trying.

**Vitamin D** is the other: a daily 10 microgram supplement is recommended right through pregnancy
and while breastfeeding, to support the baby's bones and development.

Beyond those two, a healthy varied diet covers most needs — you don't need lots of extra supplements.
One to steer clear of is **vitamin A** (retinol): don't take supplements containing it, and avoid
liver, as too much vitamin A can harm the baby.
folic-acid.when_to_see_doctor:
- A **GP, midwife, or pharmacist** can help you choose the right supplements, and some people are
  advised to take a **higher dose of folic acid** (for example with diabetes, a higher BMI, certain
  medicines, or a previous pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect) — so it's worth asking,
  especially before or in early pregnancy.

follicular-phase.title: Follicular phase
follicular-phase.glance: The follicular phase is the first half of the cycle, when an egg ripens and the womb lining thickens.
follicular-phase.overview:
The follicular phase is the first part of the cycle. It begins on the first day of your period and
runs up to ovulation. Its name comes from the follicle — the small fluid-filled sac in the ovary
that holds and grows an egg during this time.

Through this phase the hormone estrogen rises. That rising estrogen does two main things: it helps
a follicle in the ovary mature, and it thickens the lining of the uterus (womb), getting the body
ready in case a pregnancy begins later in the cycle.

Because estrogen is climbing, some people notice more energy or changes in cervical mucus as the
fertile days approach. Everyone's experience is different, and none of it needs "managing" — it's
simply the first half of your cycle doing its work.
follicular-phase.deep:
The follicular phase can vary in length from cycle to cycle, which is part of why whole cycles
differ from person to person and month to month. It ends when rising estrogen helps trigger the
release of an egg (ovulation). Because its final days lead into ovulation, this is when the fertile
window opens — which is why the end of the follicular phase matters for anyone tracking fertility.

foods-to-avoid.title: Foods to avoid in pregnancy
foods-to-avoid.glance: Most foods are fine in pregnancy — a few are worth avoiding, and it helps to keep caffeine low.
foods-to-avoid.overview:
The good news is that most foods are perfectly fine in pregnancy — only a small number are worth
avoiding or taking care with, mostly to steer clear of bugs like listeria or too much of certain
vitamins. Knowing the short list means you can relax about the rest.

The NHS advises taking care with:

- **Some cheeses** — mould-ripened soft cheeses like brie and camembert, and soft blue cheeses,
  unless they're cooked until steaming hot; and anything made with **unpasteurised** milk.
- **Raw or undercooked meat**, cold cured meats, **pâté**, and **liver** (which is very high in
  vitamin A).
- **Raw or runny eggs**, unless they carry the British Lion mark.
- **Some fish** — avoid shark, swordfish and marlin, limit tuna, and have no more than two portions
  of oily fish a week.
- **Caffeine** — keep it under about 200mg a day (roughly two mugs of instant coffee), counting tea,
  cola, energy drinks and chocolate too.
foods-to-avoid.when_to_see_doctor:
- This is general guidance, not a strict diet — if you have questions about what's safe for you, or
  a specific dietary need, your **midwife** can talk it through.
- If you've eaten something on the "avoid" list, try not to panic; mention it to your midwife if
  you're worried or feel unwell.

fsh.title: Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)
fsh.glance: FSH is a brain hormone that prompts follicles in the ovary to grow at the start of each cycle.
fsh.overview:
FSH — follicle-stimulating hormone — is one of the messenger hormones that get the cycle going.
It's made by a small gland in the brain (the pituitary) and, as its name says, it stimulates
follicles: the tiny fluid-filled sacs in the ovary that each hold an egg.

Early in the cycle, FSH encourages a group of these follicles to start growing. As a follicle
develops it releases more estrogen, which in turn thickens the lining of the uterus (womb) ready
for a possible pregnancy. Usually one follicle becomes the dominant one that goes on toward
ovulation.

FSH rises and falls as part of the normal back-and-forth of the cycle. You don't feel FSH directly
— it works quietly in the background, setting up the more visible changes of the follicular phase.
fsh.deep:
FSH works as a pair with luteinizing hormone (LH); both are released by the pituitary gland in the
brain and together they drive the ovaries through the cycle. FSH leads the first half, growing the
follicles, while the LH surge later marks the mid-cycle release of an egg. This partnership is also
why fertility treatments use FSH-based medicines: giving extra FSH encourages several follicles to
mature at once, rather than the single one a natural cycle usually produces.

gestational-diabetes.title: Gestational diabetes
gestational-diabetes.glance: Gestational diabetes is raised blood sugar during pregnancy — usually found by screening, and it often settles after birth.
gestational-diabetes.overview:
Gestational diabetes is high blood sugar (glucose) that develops during pregnancy, when the body
can't quite keep up with the extra demand for insulin. For most people it goes away again after the
baby is born.

It usually causes **no symptoms**, so it's picked up through a screening test offered in pregnancy
(a glucose tolerance test, often around 24 to 28 weeks), especially if you have things that raise the
chance of it — like a higher weight, a family history of diabetes, a previous large baby, or certain
ethnic backgrounds.

It's very manageable. Keeping blood sugar in a healthy range — through food, activity, and sometimes
medicine, all guided by your care team — lowers the chance of complications for you and your baby,
which is why it's worth staying on top of.
gestational-diabetes.when_to_see_doctor:
- Take up the **screening test** if it's offered — since gestational diabetes usually has no
  symptoms, testing is how it's found.
- Don't wait for the test if you notice possible signs of high blood sugar — feeling very thirsty,
  needing to pee a lot, a dry mouth, or tiredness — mention them to your midwife or doctor.

group-b-strep.title: Group B strep (GBS)
group-b-strep.glance: Group B strep is a common, usually harmless bacterium — the small risk is to the baby during birth, and it's manageable.
group-b-strep.overview:
Group B strep (GBS) is a very common bacterium that lots of people carry, usually in the vagina or
bottom, without knowing and without it causing any harm. It isn't a sexually transmitted infection,
and carrying it is normal.

In pregnancy it matters only because there's a **small chance** it can pass to the baby around the
time of birth and, rarely, make them unwell — this happens in roughly 1 in 1,750 pregnancies. It's
often found by chance, for example on a urine test or a vaginal swab done for another reason (the NHS
doesn't routinely screen everyone for it).

The reassuring part is that it's very manageable: if GBS is known about, having **antibiotics through
a drip during labour** greatly lowers the chance of the baby becoming ill.
group-b-strep.when_to_see_doctor:
- If you're told you carry group B strep — now or in a past pregnancy — **let your midwife or
  maternity team know**, so antibiotics during labour can be planned. It's a simple step that makes a
  real difference.

heartburn-in-pregnancy.title: Heartburn & indigestion in pregnancy
heartburn-in-pregnancy.glance: Heartburn is very common in pregnancy — usually harmless, and often eased by small everyday changes.
heartburn-in-pregnancy.overview:
Heartburn and indigestion — a burning feeling or discomfort in the chest, often after eating — are
very common in pregnancy. It's down to pregnancy hormones softening the muscle at the top of the
stomach, and, later on, the growing baby pressing upwards. It's uncomfortable, but not harmful.

Small changes often help: eating smaller meals more often rather than large ones, sitting up while
you eat and for a while afterwards, easing off spicy, fatty or caffeinated things, and not eating
late before bed. Some people find sleeping propped up a little more comfortable.

If that's not enough, a **pharmacist** can suggest antacid remedies that are safe to use in
pregnancy — a good first port of call before it becomes a bigger bother.
heartburn-in-pregnancy.when_to_see_doctor:
- See your **GP or midwife** if simple changes and pharmacy remedies aren't helping, or if you have
  **trouble swallowing**, keep bringing food back up, lose weight without meaning to, or have tummy
  pain — these are worth checking rather than putting down to ordinary heartburn.

heavy-periods.title: Heavy periods
heavy-periods.glance: Heavy periods mean losing a lot of blood each cycle — common, but worth checking if it affects you.
heavy-periods.overview:
Heavy periods — the medical name is menorrhagia — means losing a lot of blood during your periods.
For some people heavy bleeding is simply their normal, but if it's disrupting your life or leaving
you drained, it's worth looking into.

Some signs that periods are on the heavy side: needing to change a pad or tampon every 1 to 2 hours,
using two types of period product together (like a tampon and a pad), bleeding through to your
clothes or bedding, passing blood clots larger than about 2.5cm (roughly a 10p coin), or periods
that last more than 7 days.

Losing a lot of blood month after month can leave you tired or short of breath, because it can lead
to low iron (anaemia). There are many possible causes — from fibroids or conditions like
endometriosis, adenomyosis or PCOS, to some medicines — and often no serious cause is found. Either
way, heavy periods can usually be helped, so they're not something you have to just live with.
heavy-periods.when_to_see_doctor:
See a GP if:

- heavy periods are affecting your everyday life
- you're bleeding heavily for many hours, or your periods last a long time
- you also have severe period pain, or pain during sex, peeing, or pooing
- you have bleeding between periods or after sex
- you often feel tired or short of breath (this can be a sign of low iron)

A GP can look for a cause and talk through what might help.
heavy-periods.red_flags:
- Get **urgent** medical help — call **NHS 111**, or **999 / go to A&E** if it's severe — if you're
  **bleeding so heavily you soak through a pad or more every hour for a few hours in a row**, or you
  feel **faint, dizzy, or short of breath**. These can be signs of losing too much blood.

lh.title: Luteinizing hormone (LH)
lh.glance: LH is the brain hormone whose mid-cycle surge triggers the ovary to release an egg.
lh.overview:
LH — luteinizing hormone — is the messenger that sets off ovulation. Like FSH, it's made by a
small gland in the brain (the pituitary) and it tells the ovary when to release an egg.

For most of the first half of the cycle LH stays low. Then, around the middle of the cycle, it
rises sharply in what's called the LH surge. This surge is the signal that causes the ovary to
release its egg — ovulation — usually a day or so later.

The surge is a brief, well-timed signal rather than something you'd notice in how you feel. Because
it comes so closely before the egg is released, the timing of the LH rise is a reliable marker of
the most fertile part of the cycle.
lh.deep:
LH works together with FSH, the hormone that grows the follicles earlier in the cycle. Where FSH
leads the build-up, the LH surge is the turning point: levels begin climbing roughly a day and a
half before the egg is released and peak about half a day before it. After the surge, the cycle
moves into its second half. This tight timing is why LH is such a useful marker for anyone tracking
ovulation, and why it's central to how fertility treatments are planned.

luteal-phase.title: Luteal phase
luteal-phase.glance: The luteal phase is the second half of the cycle, after ovulation, when progesterone rises.
luteal-phase.overview:
The luteal phase is the part of the cycle that follows ovulation and runs until your next period
begins. It's named after the corpus luteum — the small structure the ovary forms from the empty
follicle once the egg has been released.

In this phase the hormone progesterone rises. Its job is to keep the lining of the uterus (womb)
thick and settled, so that if a fertilised egg arrives it has somewhere to implant. Estrogen stays
part of the picture too, working alongside progesterone.

If no pregnancy begins, the corpus luteum breaks down, progesterone and estrogen fall, and the
lining is no longer maintained — which brings on your next period and starts a new cycle. This is
also the stretch when some people notice premenstrual changes in mood, sleep or the body.
luteal-phase.deep:
The luteal phase tends to be a little steadier in length than the first half of the cycle, often
running somewhere in the region of about two weeks, though there's normal variation from person to
person. Because its end is tied to the fall in progesterone, the arrival of a period is really the
visible sign that hormone levels have dropped. Tracking how you feel across the luteal phase can
help you tell apart what's a familiar pattern for you from what's new or worth a conversation with
a clinician.

menopause.title: Menopause
menopause.glance: Menopause is when periods stop for good — a natural stage, usually reached between about 45 and 55.
menopause.overview:
Menopause is the point when your periods stop permanently. Because periods can come and go for a
while first, it's counted as reached once you've gone 12 months in a row without one. It usually
happens between about 45 and 55, though it can be earlier or later.

It's a natural part of ageing, not an illness. It happens as the ovaries wind down and the level of
estrogen — a key hormone of the cycle — falls. That hormonal shift is behind the changes many
people notice: hot flushes and night sweats, changes to periods in the lead-up, trouble sleeping,
shifts in mood or anxiety, brain fog, vaginal dryness, and aches.

Experiences vary enormously — some people sail through, others find it hard, and symptoms can last
several years. None of it means something is wrong with you. Support and options exist, and
understanding what's happening is a good first step.
menopause.deep:
The years of change leading up to menopause are called perimenopause; menopause itself is a single
point in time (that 12-months-without-a-period mark), and the time after is sometimes called
postmenopause. Because estrogen also affects bones and the heart over the long term, clinicians pay
attention to those alongside day-to-day symptoms. A range of approaches — from lifestyle to
non-hormonal and hormonal treatments — can ease symptoms, and what's right depends on your health,
history and preferences, which is a conversation to have with a clinician.
menopause.when_to_see_doctor:
- See a GP if menopause symptoms are troubling you or affecting daily life, and you'd like to talk
  through your options.
- **Always** see a GP if you have **any vaginal bleeding after 12 months without a period**
  (bleeding after menopause). It's often nothing serious, but it should always be checked.
- It's also worth checking in if you're bleeding more rather than less than before, or your periods
  change in a way that worries you.

menstrual-cycle.title: The menstrual cycle
menstrual-cycle.glance: The menstrual cycle is the monthly rhythm your body runs on to prepare for a possible pregnancy.
menstrual-cycle.overview:
The menstrual cycle is counted from the first day of your period — that's day 1 — up to the day
before your next period starts. It's driven by hormones that rise and fall in a repeating pattern
each month.

A cycle is often around 28 days, but that's just an average. Anywhere from about 21 to 35 days is
normal, and your own length can vary a little from month to month. Learning your own pattern is
more useful than comparing it to a number.

Across the cycle your body moves through a few stages: your period, the build-up to releasing an
egg, the release itself (ovulation), and the stretch afterwards. Each stage is shaped by
hormones, mainly estrogen and progesterone.
menstrual-cycle.deep:
The whole cycle is a conversation between the brain and the ovaries, carried by hormones. In the
first half, estrogen rises as an egg-containing follicle matures in the ovary and the lining of
the uterus (womb) thickens. Around the middle of the cycle an egg is released. In the second half,
progesterone helps keep that lining ready in case a fertilised egg arrives.

If there's no pregnancy, estrogen and progesterone fall to low levels, the lining is shed as your
period, and the pattern begins again. Because these hormones touch many systems, you may notice
small day-to-day changes across the month — this is the normal rhythm of the cycle, not something
to "fix."

menstrual-phase.title: Menstrual phase (your period)
menstrual-phase.glance: Your period is the few days of bleeding that begin each cycle, as the womb lining is shed.
menstrual-phase.overview:
The menstrual phase is your period — the days when you bleed. It starts on day 1 of the cycle,
when the levels of estrogen and progesterone have dropped low enough that the lining built up
inside the uterus (womb) is no longer maintained and comes away, leaving the body through the
vagina.

A period usually lasts about 2 to 7 days, with roughly 5 days being typical. Flow is often
heaviest in the first couple of days and lighter after that. Periods commonly begin around age 12,
though starting earlier or later is also normal.

What's "normal" varies a lot from person to person. Tracking your own periods helps you notice
what's usual for you, which is far more meaningful than any average.
menstrual-phase.deep:
The bleeding of a period is the lining of the uterus (the endometrium) being shed after a cycle
where no pregnancy has begun. It marks both the end of one cycle and the start of the next, which
is why day 1 of your period is counted as day 1 of the whole cycle. As your period finishes,
estrogen begins to rise again and the body starts rebuilding the lining for the cycle ahead.

miscarriage.title: Miscarriage
miscarriage.glance: Miscarriage is the loss of a pregnancy before 24 weeks — it's common, and almost never something you caused.
miscarriage.overview:
A miscarriage is the loss of a pregnancy in the first 24 weeks. It's more common than many people
realise, and one of the most important things to know is that it's almost never caused by anything
you did or didn't do — it usually happens because of a problem in how the pregnancy was developing,
which was outside anyone's control.

The most common signs are vaginal bleeding, and cramping or pain low in your tummy. Bleeding in
early pregnancy doesn't always mean a miscarriage is happening — many people bleed a little and go
on to have a healthy pregnancy — but it should always be checked.

However a loss happens, the feelings that come with it are real and valid, and grief is a normal
response. You don't have to go through it alone — support is available, from your midwife or GP and
from dedicated pregnancy-loss charities.
miscarriage.when_to_see_doctor:
- Contact your GP, midwife, or early pregnancy unit (or call NHS 111) if you have **vaginal bleeding
  or spotting in pregnancy**, even if it's light and there's little or no pain — so it can be
  checked.
- Ask about your nearest **early pregnancy unit**, which is set up for exactly this.
miscarriage.red_flags:
- Call **999 or go to A&E** if, in pregnancy, you have **severe tummy pain, pain in the tip of your
  shoulder, heavy bleeding, or you feel faint or very unwell**. These can be signs of a serious
  problem such as an ectopic pregnancy that needs urgent care.

morning-sickness.title: Morning sickness
morning-sickness.glance: Feeling or being sick is very common in early pregnancy, and usually eases by around weeks 16 to 20.
morning-sickness.overview:
Feeling sick, or being sick, is very common in early pregnancy. Despite the name "morning sickness,"
it can happen at any time of the day or night. For most people it starts in the first few weeks and
settles down by around 16 to 20 weeks.

It's unpleasant, and for some it really affects day-to-day life — but ordinary morning sickness does
not put your baby at any increased risk. Eating small amounts often, and finding what helps you, can
make it more bearable; a midwife, GP or pharmacist can suggest safe options if you're struggling.

For a small number of people the sickness becomes severe (this is called hyperemesis gravidarum),
with a real risk of becoming dehydrated. That version needs medical help — see the signs below.
morning-sickness.when_to_see_doctor:
Contact your midwife, GP, or NHS 111 if you:

- cannot keep any food or drink down for 24 hours
- have very dark urine, or do not pee for more than 8 hours
- feel very weak, dizzy, or faint when you stand up
- have tummy pain, a high temperature, or you're vomiting blood
- are losing weight
morning-sickness.red_flags:
- Being unable to keep fluids down, with very dark or no urine, can mean you're getting dehydrated
  (severe pregnancy sickness) — **contact your midwife, GP or NHS 111 the same day**, as you may
  need treatment to stop it getting worse.

ovulation.title: Ovulation
ovulation.glance: Ovulation is when an ovary releases an egg — the most fertile point of your cycle.
ovulation.overview:
Ovulation is the moment an ovary releases a mature egg. It's the turning point of the cycle: the
first half builds up to it, and the second half follows it.

In a cycle of about 28 days, ovulation often happens around day 14 — but the timing varies. A
helpful way to think about it is that ovulation usually occurs somewhere from 10 to 16 days before
your next period starts. It can be hard to pinpoint the exact day.

Once released, an egg can be fertilised for only about 12 to 24 hours. Sperm, though, can survive
in the body for several days, so the "fertile window" is wider than a single day — roughly the few
days leading up to ovulation and the day itself.
ovulation.deep:
The release of the egg is triggered by a short, sharp rise in hormones around mid-cycle, following
the estrogen build-up of the follicular phase. Because sperm can live for a number of days while
the egg lives less than a day, pregnancy is most likely from sex in the days just before
ovulation. Ovulation can shift from cycle to cycle with things like stress or illness, which is
why predicting it exactly is difficult and why tracking several cycles is more reliable than any
single calculation.

pain-during-sex.title: Pain during sex
pain-during-sex.glance: Pain during sex is common, has many possible causes, and is always worth getting checked — help exists.
pain-during-sex.overview:
Pain during sex — sometimes called dyspareunia — is more common than many people realise, and it's
never something you simply have to accept. It can have many causes, and finding the right one is the
key to easing it.

Some causes are physical. Vaginal dryness is a frequent one, often linked to hormones around
menopause or to not enough arousal, and it can make sex feel sore or uncomfortable. Infections, such
as thrush, can also cause pain. Another cause is vaginismus — when the muscles around the vagina
tighten on their own as penetration is attempted, which can make sex painful or feel impossible.
This is involuntary, it's not "in your head," and it's treatable.

Because the cause can be physical, hormonal, or linked to how relaxed or aroused you feel — and
often a mix — the useful step is to have it looked at rather than to guess or to soldier on.
pain-during-sex.when_to_see_doctor:
- See a GP or a sexual health clinic if sex is painful — whatever the cause, it's worth checking,
  and there's effective help for the common causes.
- It can feel awkward to raise, but clinicians deal with this often and are there to help, not to
  judge. You can ask for a female doctor, bring someone with you, and talk through what would make
  an examination comfortable.
- Do get any bleeding after sex checked, and see someone sooner if the pain is severe or you also
  feel unwell.

pain-relief-in-labour.title: Pain relief in labour
pain-relief-in-labour.glance: There are several ways to ease labour pain — there's no right or wrong choice, and you can stay flexible.
pain-relief-in-labour.overview:
Labour is different for everyone, and there are several ways to cope with the pain — from simple
comfort measures to medical options. Knowing what's available ahead of time can help you feel more
prepared.

Options range from **staying active and upright**, breathing and relaxation, massage, and being in
**water** (a bath or birth pool), through to **a TENS machine**, **gas and air** (Entonox, which you
breathe yourself), **injections** like pethidine, and an **epidural** (given by an anaesthetist,
which numbs the pain of labour more fully).

There's no "best" choice — it depends on you, your labour, and how you feel on the day. It's worth
noting your preferences in a **birth plan**, while keeping an open mind: many people find they want
more, or less, pain relief than they expected, and that's completely fine.
pain-relief-in-labour.when_to_see_doctor:
- Your **midwife** (and, for an epidural, an anaesthetist) will talk you through the options and help
  you decide what suits you — during pregnancy and again during labour itself. There's no need to
  decide everything in advance.

pcos.title: PCOS (polycystic ovary syndrome)
pcos.glance: PCOS is a common hormonal condition that can affect periods, ovulation, skin and hair.
pcos.overview:
PCOS — polycystic ovary syndrome — is a common condition linked to the balance of reproductive
hormones. Estimates suggest it affects somewhere around 1 in 10 women of reproductive age, and many
people who have it are never diagnosed.

It can show up in different ways, and no two people are quite the same. Common features include
periods that are irregular, infrequent, or absent; higher levels of hormones called androgens,
which can lead to extra hair growth on the face or body, acne, or thinning hair on the scalp; and
ovaries that don't release an egg as regularly as usual, which can make it harder to conceive.
Weight changes and patches of darker skin are also common.

The exact cause isn't fully understood, and there's no cure — but the symptoms can be managed, and
understanding what's happening is the first step. PCOS is common and manageable, not something to
feel ashamed of.
pcos.deep:
Because PCOS involves the body's hormones and how it handles insulin, it's also linked over the
longer term to insulin resistance and a higher chance of type 2 diabetes, raised blood pressure,
and changes in cholesterol — which is why clinicians tend to keep an eye on these things over time.
Roughly half of people with PCOS may develop diabetes or pre-diabetes by their forties, so regular
check-ins matter. Diagnosis isn't something to self-assess: a clinician looks at the overall
picture — your history and periods, sometimes blood tests for hormones, and sometimes an ultrasound
of the ovaries — and rules out other causes before reaching PCOS.
pcos.when_to_see_doctor:
It's worth seeing a GP if you notice things that fit the picture above, especially if they're
affecting how you feel day to day:

- periods that are irregular, very infrequent, or have stopped
- noticeably more hair growth on the face or body, persistent acne, or scalp hair thinning
- difficulty getting pregnant after trying for a while
- weight gain that's hard to shift, alongside other symptoms

A GP can look into what's going on, confirm whether it's PCOS or something else, and talk through a
plan that fits you. PCOS is also linked with low mood and anxiety — if you're struggling with how
you feel, tell your GP too; that's part of the picture and support is available.

perimenopause.title: Perimenopause
perimenopause.glance: Perimenopause is the transition leading up to menopause, when periods and hormones start to change.
perimenopause.overview:
Perimenopause is the stretch of time leading up to menopause — the "around menopause" years. It
begins when you first notice the changes and runs until a full year after your last period, at
which point you've reached menopause. It can last several years.

During this time the ovaries gradually make less estrogen, and levels rise and fall less
predictably than before. The most common early sign is that periods change — becoming closer
together or further apart, lighter or heavier. Many of the symptoms linked with menopause, such as
hot flushes, sleep changes, or shifts in mood, can begin here while you're still having periods.

Because it's gradual and varies so much, perimenopause can be confusing — the changes don't arrive
all at once or in the same order for everyone. Knowing this phase has a name, and that it's a
normal transition, can make it easier to make sense of.
perimenopause.when_to_see_doctor:
- See a GP if perimenopause symptoms are affecting your daily life and you'd like to talk through
  what might help.
- It's worth getting checked if your periods become very heavy, or if you have bleeding between
  periods or after sex, so the cause can be found.
- Remember that pregnancy can still happen during perimenopause, so it's worth raising
  contraception with a clinician if that's relevant for you.

period-pain.title: Period pain
period-pain.glance: Period pain is cramping in your lower tummy around your period — common, and often a normal part of the cycle.
period-pain.overview:
Period pain is the cramping, aching feeling in your lower tummy that many people get around their
period. It happens when the muscular wall of the womb tightens, and it's often a normal part of the
menstrual cycle. The medical name for it is dysmenorrhea.

It usually comes on at the start of your period, or just before, and tends to last up to about
three days. For some it's a mild heaviness; for others the cramps are stronger. Pain can also
change over your life and from cycle to cycle.

Period pain that follows this familiar pattern is common and usually manageable. Everyday comfort
measures and simple painkillers are what many people use, and a pharmacist or GP can advise on what
might suit you. What matters is knowing your own usual pattern — so you can notice if something
changes.
period-pain.when_to_see_doctor:
It's worth talking to a GP if:

- your periods become more painful, heavier, or more irregular than usual
- the pain stops you doing everyday things like work or school
- ordinary painkillers don't help
- you have pain during sex, or when peeing or pooing
- you bleed between periods
- your pain comes at times other than just before or during your period
- you pass blood clots larger than a coin (about the size of a quarter)
- you also notice a swollen tummy, less appetite, or weight loss you can't explain

These don't mean something is wrong, but they're worth checking — period pain that's new,
different, or hard to manage can have causes a clinician can help with.
period-pain.red_flags:
- Ask for an **urgent** GP appointment or call **NHS 111** if your period or pelvic pain is
  **severe, or worse than usual, and painkillers have not helped.**

planning-pregnancy.title: Planning a pregnancy
planning-pregnancy.glance: A few simple steps before trying — folic acid, stopping smoking and alcohol — give a pregnancy the best start.
planning-pregnancy.overview:
If you're thinking about trying for a baby, a handful of steps beforehand can give a pregnancy a
healthier start — many of them working from before you even conceive.

The main ones: start taking **folic acid** (and vitamin D), **stop smoking**, and **avoid alcohol**.
Aiming for a healthy weight helps too, as being significantly under- or over-weight can make it
harder to conceive. It's also worth making sure your **MMR vaccination** is up to date, since some
infections can affect a pregnancy.

None of this needs to be perfect or stressful. Small, kind changes ahead of time are what matter —
and getting a bit of a head start is one of the nicest things you can do for a future pregnancy.
planning-pregnancy.when_to_see_doctor:
- If you have a **long-term health condition** or take **regular medicine**, see your GP before you
  start trying — some conditions and medicines need planning around. **Don't stop any prescribed
  medicine** without talking to your doctor first.
- A GP can also advise on folic acid (including whether you need a higher dose) and getting to a
  healthy weight before pregnancy.

postnatal-depression.title: Postnatal depression
postnatal-depression.glance: Postnatal depression is a common, treatable low mood after birth — it's not your fault, and help is there.
postnatal-depression.overview:
Feeling down, anxious, or irritable in the first couple of weeks after birth is very common — this
is often called the "baby blues," and it usually passes on its own within about two weeks.

Postnatal depression is different: a low mood that's deeper or lasts longer. It's a common condition,
it can start any time in the first year, and it can affect fathers and partners too. Signs include a
persistent low mood, finding it hard to enjoy anything, trouble sleeping even when your baby sleeps,
and sometimes difficult feelings about bonding with your baby.

Having it does **not** mean you're a bad parent or that you don't love your baby — it's an illness,
not a failing, and it responds well to support and treatment. Reaching out early is a strong, caring
thing to do, for you and your baby.
postnatal-depression.when_to_see_doctor:
- Speak to your **GP, midwife, or health visitor** if you think you might have postnatal depression,
  or if the "baby blues" haven't lifted after two weeks. They will have seen it many times and can
  help you find the right support.
postnatal-depression.red_flags:
- If you have **thoughts of harming yourself or your baby**, or that your family would be better off
  without you, get help **right away**: call **999** or go to A&E, or call **NHS 111** or the
  Samaritans on **116 123**. These thoughts can be part of the illness, they are not who you are, and
  urgent help is available.

pre-eclampsia.title: Pre-eclampsia
pre-eclampsia.glance: Pre-eclampsia is raised blood pressure in pregnancy — often silent at first, which is why antenatal checks matter.
pre-eclampsia.overview:
Pre-eclampsia is a condition of pregnancy that mainly shows up as high blood pressure, along with
protein in the urine. It usually appears from around 20 weeks, and sometimes after the birth.

One of the most important things to know is that early on it often causes **no symptoms at all** —
you can feel completely fine. That's exactly why your midwife checks your blood pressure and tests
your urine at every routine antenatal appointment: those checks are how it's usually picked up
before you'd notice anything.

When symptoms do come, they're worth knowing, because pre-eclampsia can become serious for both you
and your baby. It's very treatable when caught, and keeping up with your antenatal appointments is
the single best way to stay ahead of it.
pre-eclampsia.when_to_see_doctor:
- Keep all your **routine antenatal appointments** — the blood-pressure and urine checks are how
  pre-eclampsia is usually found before symptoms start.
pre-eclampsia.red_flags:
Get medical help **immediately** — contact your maternity unit, or call **NHS 111** — if you have
any of these (call **999** if you're seriously unwell, for example a fit/seizure):

- a **severe headache** that doesn't ease with ordinary painkillers
- **vision problems** — blurring or flashing lights
- **sudden swelling** of your face, hands, or feet
- **pain just below your ribs**
- being **sick**, or suddenly feeling very unwell

pregnancy.title: Pregnancy
pregnancy.glance: Pregnancy usually lasts about 40 weeks, counted from the first day of your last period.
pregnancy.overview:
Pregnancy is the time your body grows and carries a baby. It normally lasts about 40 weeks —
anywhere from 37 to 42 weeks is considered full and normal — and, perhaps surprisingly, it's counted
from the first day of your **last period**, not from conception. That's just the standard way dates
are worked out.

Your **due date** is an estimate, not a deadline: babies happily arrive a bit earlier or later. Early
in pregnancy a "dating scan" (usually around 12 weeks) can measure your baby and give a more accurate
date, which sometimes shifts the original estimate.

Pregnancy is often talked about in three stages, or **trimesters**, each with its own changes. All
the way through, you're looked after with regular antenatal check-ups from a midwife (and a doctor if
needed) — the care that helps keep you and your baby well.
pregnancy.deep:
Because dates are counted from the last period, you're considered around four weeks pregnant by the
time a period is missed. The weeks-of-pregnancy count is how care is organised — scans, screening,
and check-ups are all offered at particular weeks. If your periods are irregular or you're unsure of
dates, the dating scan is what sets the timeline. This atom is the map of the whole journey; the
specific topics — signs of pregnancy, antenatal care, keeping well, and labour — each have their own.

pregnancy-test.title: Pregnancy test
pregnancy-test.glance: A home pregnancy test checks your urine for the pregnancy hormone hCG — most reliable from the first missed period.
pregnancy-test.overview:
A home pregnancy test works by detecting a hormone called hCG (human chorionic gonadotrophin) in
your urine. Your body starts making it a few days after a fertilised egg implants, and the amount
rises quickly in early pregnancy.

The test is most reliable from the **first day of a missed period** — roughly two weeks after
conception. If your cycle is irregular or you're not sure when your period is due, waiting until at
least 21 days after unprotected sex gives a more dependable result. You don't need to test first
thing in the morning; any time of day is fine.

A **positive** result is almost certainly right — very few tests show positive when you're not
pregnant. A **negative** result is a little less certain: if your period still doesn't arrive and you
think you might be pregnant, wait a few days and test again.
pregnancy-test.when_to_see_doctor:
- If you get a positive result, contact a **midwife or GP** to begin antenatal care.
- If tests are negative but your period is missing and you feel pregnant (or unwell), see a GP to
  find out what's happening.

premature-labour.title: Premature labour
premature-labour.glance: Premature labour is labour before 37 weeks — act quickly, as early care makes a real difference.
premature-labour.overview:
Premature (or preterm) labour is labour that starts before the 37th week of pregnancy. It happens in
roughly 8 in 100 births.

Babies born early are more vulnerable, but many go on to do well — especially with the specialist
care that neonatal units provide. The key is acting quickly if you think it might be starting, so you
can be assessed and, if needed, given treatments that help protect the baby.

The signs are similar to labour at any stage, but before 37 weeks they should never be waited out —
they're always a reason to make contact straight away.
premature-labour.when_to_see_doctor:
- Call your **midwife or maternity unit** any time you're **less than 37 weeks** and unsure or
  worried — it's always okay to check.
premature-labour.red_flags:
Contact your **midwife or maternity unit immediately** — day or night — if, **before 37 weeks**, you
have any of these:

- regular **contractions or tightenings**, or period-type pains
- a **gush or trickle of fluid** from your vagina (your waters breaking)
- **backache** that's not usual for you, or a feeling of pressure low down

premenstrual-syndrome.title: PMS (premenstrual syndrome)
premenstrual-syndrome.glance: PMS is the mix of physical and emotional changes many people notice in the week or two before a period.
premenstrual-syndrome.overview:
PMS — premenstrual syndrome — is the name for the changes many people feel in the days or couple of
weeks before their period. It can affect anyone who has periods, and it usually eases within a few
days after the period starts.

The changes come in many forms. Physically, you might notice bloating, sore or tender breasts,
cramps, headaches, or feeling more tired. Emotionally, there can be mood swings, irritability,
anxiety, or feeling low. Food cravings and changes in sleep are common too. Not everyone gets PMS,
and those who do won't get every symptom — your own pattern is what matters.

PMS is a normal, recognised part of many people's cycles, tied to the natural hormonal shifts of
the second half. Noticing how it shows up for you, cycle to cycle, can make it easier to plan
around — and to spot if it ever changes.
premenstrual-syndrome.when_to_see_doctor:
It's worth talking to a GP if:

- your symptoms are affecting your daily life — work, studies, relationships
- everyday changes to your routine haven't helped
- your low mood, anxiety, or irritability feels severe

A clinician can talk through what might help. A more intense form, called premenstrual dysphoric
disorder (PMDD), can cause much stronger mood symptoms, and support is available for it.
premenstrual-syndrome.red_flags:
- If you have symptoms of PMDD and are **feeling suicidal or that you cannot keep yourself safe**,
  get help straight away: **call 999 or go to A&E.** Don't drive yourself — ask someone to take
  you, or ask for an ambulance. You deserve support, and help is available.

progesterone.title: Progesterone
progesterone.glance: Progesterone is the hormone of the cycle's second half, preparing the womb lining after ovulation.
progesterone.overview:
Progesterone is one of the main hormones behind the menstrual cycle, and it takes the lead in the
second half — after an egg is released at ovulation.

Its main role is to help the lining of the uterus (womb) stay thick and ready, so that if a
fertilised egg arrives it can implant and a pregnancy can begin. In this way progesterone works as
a partner to estrogen, which did much of the build-up earlier in the cycle.

If no pregnancy begins, progesterone levels fall. That drop is what allows the lining to be shed
as your next period. The rise and fall of progesterone across the second half of the cycle is a
normal, expected rhythm.
progesterone.deep:
Progesterone is produced mainly by the corpus luteum — the structure the ovary forms from the
follicle after it has released its egg. This is why progesterone rises specifically in the luteal
(post-ovulation) phase. When the corpus luteum breaks down, progesterone and estrogen both fall,
signalling the start of a new cycle. Its natural shifts are part of why some people notice
premenstrual changes in the days before a period.

progestogen-only-pill.title: The progestogen-only pill (mini pill)
progestogen-only-pill.glance: The mini pill is a daily pill with one hormone that thickens cervical mucus to block sperm.
progestogen-only-pill.overview:
The progestogen-only pill — often called the mini pill — is a daily tablet containing just one
hormone, a progestogen. It's an option for people who can't or would rather not take estrogen.

Its main action is to thicken the mucus at the neck of the womb, so sperm find it harder to reach an
egg. One common type, the desogestrel pill, also stops the ovaries from releasing an egg
(ovulation).
