Taken correctly, it's over 99% effective; with typical everyday use it's around 91%. As with other
pills, timing matters, and it doesn't protect against STIs.
progestogen-only-pill.deep:
The mini pill differs from the combined pill in having no estrogen, which changes who it may suit —
something a clinician weighs up when it's prescribed. Some types need to be taken within a fairly
tight daily window to stay effective. This atom covers what it is and how it works; how to take it
and whether it's right for you are matters for a GP, nurse, or pharmacist.

signs-of-labour.title: Signs of labour
signs-of-labour.glance: Signs that labour is starting include regular contractions, a "show," backache, or your waters breaking.
signs-of-labour.overview:
There are a few signs that labour may be starting. The main one is contractions — tightenings across
your bump that come regularly and build up. Others include a "show" (the plug of mucus from your
cervix coming away), a persistent backache, a need to go to the toilet, and your waters breaking.

Before active labour there's often an early ("latent") phase, when the cervix softens and starts to
open. This part can take hours or even days, and for many people it's fine to stay comfortable at
home during it, resting and keeping hydrated.

Everyone's labour begins a little differently, so you don't need to tick off every sign. When you
think things are starting, your midwife or maternity unit is there to guide you on what to do and
when to come in.
signs-of-labour.when_to_see_doctor:
- Call your **midwife or maternity unit** for guidance when you think labour has started, or when
  contractions are **regular — about every 5 minutes**. If you can't reach your midwife, call
  **NHS 111**.
signs-of-labour.red_flags:
Call your **midwife or maternity unit immediately** — day or night, don't wait — if:

- your **waters break** (especially if the fluid is green, brown, or smelly)
- you have **any vaginal bleeding**
- your **baby is moving less than usual**
- you have signs of labour and you're **less than 37 weeks pregnant**

signs-of-pregnancy.title: Signs of pregnancy
signs-of-pregnancy.glance: A missed period is often the first sign of pregnancy, sometimes alongside nausea, tiredness or tender breasts.
signs-of-pregnancy.overview:
For many people the first hint of pregnancy is a **missed period**. But bodies vary, and some notice
other early signs first — often around 4 to 6 weeks in.

Common early signs include feeling or being sick (at any time of day, not just the morning), breasts
that feel larger or tender, feeling unusually tired, and needing to pee more often. Some people also
notice a metallic taste, a new sensitivity to certain smells, or going off foods they normally like.

None of these on their own means you're definitely pregnant — many overlap with the ordinary ups and
downs of the cycle — and not everyone gets them. The way to know for sure is a pregnancy test.
signs-of-pregnancy.when_to_see_doctor:
- If a test is positive, contact a **midwife or GP** to start your pregnancy (antenatal) care early.
- If your period is late and tests are negative but symptoms continue, it's worth checking in with a
  GP to look at what else might be going on.

smoking-in-pregnancy.title: Smoking in pregnancy
smoking-in-pregnancy.glance: Stopping smoking is one of the best things you can do for your baby — and it's never too late.
smoking-in-pregnancy.overview:
Stopping smoking is one of the most powerful things you can do to give your baby a healthy start.
Every cigarette restricts the oxygen your baby gets, which makes their heart work harder and can
hold back their growth.

Smoking in pregnancy raises the risk of serious problems, including miscarriage, premature birth,
low birth weight, stillbirth, and sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) after the birth. Second-hand
smoke matters too, so a smoke-free home helps.

The encouraging part: it's **never too late**. Stopping at any point in pregnancy helps, and quitting
early brings the most benefit. It can be genuinely hard, which is exactly why free help exists — and
using it makes success much more likely.
smoking-in-pregnancy.when_to_see_doctor:
- Ask your **midwife** about **free NHS stop-smoking support** — trained advisers (some who
  specialise in pregnancy) can support you, and there's a Smokefree helpline too. Getting help is a
  sign of looking after your baby, not a failing.

spotting.title: Spotting & bleeding between periods
spotting.glance: Spotting is light bleeding between periods or after sex — often not serious, but always worth getting checked.
spotting.overview:
Spotting means light bleeding that happens between your periods or after sex, outside your normal
flow. It's common, and it's usually not something serious — but because it can have several causes,
it's the kind of thing that's always worth getting checked by a clinician.

There are many everyday reasons for it. Starting or using hormonal contraception is a frequent one.
Others include small, harmless growths in or around the womb (polyps or fibroids), harmless changes
to the surface of the cervix, vaginal dryness, or an infection such as chlamydia.

Because the same symptom can come from different causes — most of them minor — the useful step
isn't to guess, it's to have it looked at so you know what's behind it for you.
spotting.when_to_see_doctor:
- See a GP or a sexual health clinic **any time you have bleeding between periods or after sex**,
  even if it's light. It's usually nothing serious, but getting it checked is how the cause is
  found — and it's the way to rule out less common causes early.
spotting.red_flags:
- Ask for an **urgent** GP appointment or call **NHS 111** if you have **missed a period and have
  unusual bleeding along with tummy or pelvic pain** — this needs prompt assessment, as it can be a
  sign of an ectopic pregnancy.

stillbirth.title: Stillbirth
stillbirth.glance: Stillbirth is the loss of a baby after 24 weeks — uncommon, never your fault, and always met with support.
stillbirth.overview:
A stillbirth is when a baby is born having died after 24 weeks of pregnancy. (A loss before 24 weeks
is called a miscarriage.) It's uncommon — around 1 in every 250 births — but for the families it
touches, it is a profound loss, and everything about the care that follows is meant to hold you
gently through it.

Sometimes a cause is found — for example a problem with the placenta or the baby's development, or a
health condition — and sometimes, despite tests, **no cause is found at all**. Whatever the reason, a
stillbirth is not something a parent has caused or could have known to prevent.

One thing genuinely does help lower the risk, and it's simple: **telling your midwife straight away
if your baby's movements slow down or change.** Alongside that, the everyday things — going to
antenatal appointments, not smoking, avoiding alcohol, and sleeping on your side from 28 weeks — all
play a part.
stillbirth.when_to_see_doctor:
- Contact your **midwife or maternity unit immediately** — any time, day or night — if your **baby is
  moving less than usual or their movements feel different.** Never wait to see if it passes; getting
  checked is exactly the right thing to do, and it's never a bother.
- After a loss, specialist midwives and bereavement teams are there for you — for the decisions,
  the practical steps, and the grief. You do not have to face any of it alone, and support groups
  for baby loss are available for as long as you need them.

stress-and-your-periods.title: Stress, life & your periods
stress-and-your-periods.glance: Stress, big changes in weight, or lots of exercise can delay or stop a period — often just for a while.
stress-and-your-periods.overview:
It's common for a period to arrive late, or to skip a month, and the reason often has more to do
with life than with anything being wrong. Stress is a frequent one — the same system that responds
to pressure can nudge the hormones that run your cycle.

Other everyday things can shift your periods too: a big change in weight (up or down), doing a lot
of exercise, or being run down. Hormonal changes — such as the approach of perimenopause, or
conditions like PCOS — can also be behind it, as can pregnancy and some contraception. Often the gap
between periods simply varies a little from time to time, and that's normal.

The reassuring part is that a one-off late or missed period usually isn't a cause for concern, and
things often settle as life does. What's worth watching is a pattern of change rather than a single
month.
stress-and-your-periods.when_to_see_doctor:
See a GP if:

- you've missed **three periods in a row**, or your periods have become **irregular**
- your periods **stop** and you're not sure why (and pregnancy is possible, it's worth a test first)
- missed periods come with other changes — like unexpected weight changes, tiredness, extra hair
  growth, or feeling low

These checks are just to understand what's behind the change — which is usually something
manageable.

the-coil.title: The coil (IUD and IUS)
the-coil.glance: The coil is a small device placed in the womb — copper (IUD) or hormonal (IUS) — that lasts years.
the-coil.overview:
The coil is a small device a clinician places inside the womb. There are two kinds, and it helps to
tell them apart:

- The **IUD**, or copper coil, contains no hormones. The copper changes conditions in the womb so
  that sperm and eggs can't survive well, and it also affects cervical mucus. Depending on the type,
  it works for around 5 to 10 years.
- The **IUS**, or hormonal coil, releases a progestogen instead of using copper. It thickens the
  mucus at the neck of the womb and thins the womb lining; for some people it can also make periods
  much lighter.

Both are "fit and forget" methods and both are over 99% effective, with little difference between
perfect and typical use. Neither protects against STIs.
the-coil.deep:
The coils are long-acting reversible methods: once fitted they keep working for years, and fertility
returns after they're removed. Fitting and removal are done by a trained clinician and take only a
few minutes, though some people find fitting uncomfortable. A common reason people choose between
the two is their effect on periods — the copper IUD can make periods heavier at first, while the
hormonal IUS often makes them lighter. Which suits you is a conversation with a clinician; this atom
just explains how each works.

twin-pregnancy.title: Twin & multiple pregnancy
twin-pregnancy.glance: Carrying twins is usually first spotted at the dating scan, and means a bit more antenatal care.
twin-pregnancy.overview:
Expecting more than one baby is usually first discovered at the **dating scan** (around 12 weeks),
which can also show whether the babies share a placenta.

There are two main kinds. **Identical** twins come from a single fertilised egg that splits, so they
share the same genes and are always the same sex. **Non-identical** twins come from two separate
eggs, and are no more alike than any other siblings; they're the more common of the two, and are a
bit more likely with older age, a family history on the mother's side, or after fertility treatment.

Carrying twins or more is its own experience, and it usually means a **little more antenatal care** —
extra appointments and scans to keep a close eye on you and your babies. Your midwifery team will
explain what to expect.
twin-pregnancy.when_to_see_doctor:
- If a scan shows twins (or more), your **midwife** will talk you through the extra check-ups and
  scans that come with a multiple pregnancy — going along to them all is the best way to stay well
  looked after.

vaginal-dryness.title: Vaginal dryness
vaginal-dryness.glance: Vaginal dryness is common, often linked to hormones, and can cause soreness or discomfort during sex.
vaginal-dryness.overview:
Vaginal dryness is a common experience that many people have at some point. It happens when the
usual moisture that keeps the vagina comfortable is reduced, and it can feel like soreness,
itching, or discomfort — including pain or discomfort during sex.

It's often linked to hormones, especially a fall in estrogen. That's why it's common around
menopause and perimenopause, but it can also happen during breastfeeding, with some medicines (such
as certain contraceptives or antidepressants), or when there isn't enough arousal before sex. It's
nothing to feel embarrassed about — it's a physical thing, not a reflection of you or your
relationship.

Knowing it's common, and usually very treatable, is a good starting point. There are simple options
that can help, and a GP or pharmacist can point you to what suits you.
vaginal-dryness.when_to_see_doctor:
See a GP if:

- vaginal dryness is bothering you or doesn't settle after a few weeks
- it's affecting your daily life or your sex life
- you also have unusual discharge, or any bleeding after sex, between periods, or after menopause

There's no need to just put up with it — help is available, and a clinician can look at what's
behind it and what might ease it.

vaginal-health.title: Vaginal & vulva health
vaginal-health.glance: The vagina cleans itself — gentle care on the outside is all it needs, and discharge is normal.
vaginal-health.overview:
One of the most reassuring things to know is that the vagina looks after itself. It's naturally
self-cleaning, and the discharge you notice is part of that — a fluid that keeps it clean and moist
and helps protect it from infection. The amount and texture change through the cycle, which is
completely normal.

Because of this, the vagina doesn't need washing on the inside. In fact, washing inside it —
"douching" — can upset its natural balance. The outside (the vulva) just needs gentle care: warm
water and, if you like, a mild, non-perfumed soap. Perfumed soaps, gels, deodorants and scented
wipes are best avoided, as they can cause irritation.

Getting to know what's normal for you — your usual discharge, look and feel — makes it easier to
notice if something changes and might need checking.
vaginal-health.when_to_see_doctor:
See a GP or sexual health clinic if you notice:

- a change in your discharge — its colour, smell, or texture, or a lot more than usual
- itching, soreness, or irritation around the vagina or vulva
- bleeding between periods or after sex
- pain when peeing, or pain low down between your tummy and thighs (pelvic pain)

These are common and often easily treated — a change in discharge can simply mean a mild infection
like thrush. Getting it checked is the way to know, rather than guessing.
